newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore insurance business seen getting tougher.
newsitem.headline: Singapore insurance business seen getting tougher.

text.p: Investment conditions for life insurers will be extremely difficult over the next few years and competition in personal lines business will become more intense, the chairman of Singapore's largest insurer said on Friday.

"The investment climate continues to be extremely difficult, especially for Singapore-based funds," said Ng Pock Too, chairman of NTUC Income Insurance Co-operative Ltd (Income), Singapore's biggest composite insurer.
Ng told the company's annual general meeting that high liquidity in Singapore had reduced demand for investment funds, which had hit interest rates and investment yields.
"It is likely that investment returns will continue to be low over the next few years," he said.

Ng said Income's decision to cut 1998 life insurance policy bonus rates in April had been a necessary move, but a separate statement from Income chief executive Tan Kin Lian said there had been no adverse reaction from policyholders.
"We have not received any adverse reactions from our policyholders concerning the revision of bonus rates," Tan said.
In April, Income cut between eight and 11 percent from its 1998 life insurance bonus rates, dropping them to 2.5 and 1.0 percent from 3.5 and 2.0 percent.
The country's biggest life insurer, Great Eastern Life Assurance Ltd, also said it would cut bonus rates.
Prudential Corp and American International Assurance, the two foreign members of Singapore's "Big Four" life insurance companies, have said they plan no cuts.
Tan said between April 15 and May 15, new applications for life insurance were up 5.0 percent over the previous month and 47 percent up on the same period last year.
But Ng said competition was set to increase and would make any new business gains hard to keep in the face of growing competition from foreign insurers entering the market.
"This competition is severe in many areas, but none more so than in motor insurance," Ng said.
With a 28.5 percent share of premiums, Income is the market leader, but Ng said competition was "leading to an erosion of premium rates".
